Enterprises deploying large language models (LLMs) in production may be unknowingly footing the bill for someone else’s AI business. Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) is warning of financially motivated LLMjacking campaigns in which cybercriminals hijack enterprise cloud and model access before reselling it through underground subscription services.

The activity can generate fake cloud charges exceeding $100,000 in a single day, GTIG said in a blog post. In some incidents, cumulative charges reached $1 million before organizations revoked the compromised access.

“LLM Mixers turn stolen enterprise model access into a service for paying customers, while the victim’s systems continue accepting requests through credentials they recognize,” said Piyush Sharma, co-founder and CEO at Tuskira. “That puts a lot of weight on the authority attached to each credential. A key issued for one application shouldn’t become a reusable pass to other models and workloads.”

GTIG’s analysis is based on multiple incidents in 2026, spanning a variety of cloud and LLM providers across North America, South America, and Asia Pacific.

Stolen model access becomes an underground business

GTIG said the monetization infrastructure centers on LLM Mixers, criminal routing gateways that aggregate compromised API credentials and resell model access to underground subscribers. These services proxy requests across stolen accounts, distribute consumption and hide the original source of access.

Multiple operations were identified using open-source gateways and custom relay infrastructure to pool stolen credentials. One threat actor, UNC6993, used tools including new-api and gcli2api to aggregate stolen keys and distribute requests across accounts.

Another operation used stolen third-party API keys to power Jet Night, a legitimate token-routing service that executed more than 500,000 LLM API calls in under eight hours, GTIG said. The activity passed nearly $1 million in token costs to the victim organization. Jet Night advertises unlimited access to frontier models for approximately $60 a month, substantially lower than the typical cost of comparable legitimate access.

Jet Night also experienced occasional outages that GTIG suspects were caused by victims discovering compromises and revoking keys.

“Selling stolen model access gives criminals a reason to keep that access working for as long as possible, which makes the quiet activity before the spending spike especially important,” said Nick Tausek, lead security automation architect at Swimlane. “By the time someone asks why the cloud bill has exploded, the attacker may already have paying customers.”

The attack begins long before the bill arrives

Initial access involves exposed or stolen cloud identity tokens, including IAM credentials, service account keys, GitHub personal access tokens, and active session tokens, GTIG pointed out. Attackers also harvest LLM API keys from public repositories and scan for exposed model endpoints.

Attackers were seen validating stolen keys with minimal single-token requests, sometimes using max-tokens=1. Such micro-transactions can confirm whether credentials work while remaining below conventional consumption-based detection thresholds.

“Testing a stolen key with a single-token request barely registers as consumption,” Tausek said. “But pair that request with a newly created credential or an unexpected permission change, and there’s something worth investigating.” Analysts shouldn’t have to pull those connections together manually while the attacker gets a head start, he added.

After establishing access, attackers enumerate cloud services, repositories, and data stores for additional credentials. They may escalate privileges, create unauthorized service accounts, inject SSH keys, or establish persistence through compromised workloads.

GTIG observed a follow-on threat actor exploiting a user ID rebinding vulnerability in the LiteLLM gateway to elevate ordinary virtual keys into administrative credentials.

Sharma said organizations must restrict credentials to their intended models, workloads, and endpoints. “The gateway compromise described in these incidents deserves particular attention,” he said, warning that control of the routing layer could open access beyond the original compromised credential.

GTIG recommends tighter credential management, least-privilege permissions, granular API key scopes, monitoring for suspicious low-volume requests, and spending limits on model consumption. It also urges organizations to monitor unauthorized AI service enablement and gateway vulnerabilities.

In this article

Fashion retailer Revolve said customers’ payment card numbers and expiration dates were stolen

Data at risk includes card numbers and expiration dates, customer names and addresses

Affected customers should watch their statements and consider asking issuers for new cards

Online fashion retailer Revolve Group said customers’ payment card numbers and expiration dates were stolen. In its customer notification letter filed with the Massachusetts Attorney General, Revolve told recipients the incident involved their names, addresses, and payment card details.

What was stolen?

The at-risk data includes customer names and contact information, payment card numbers, and card expiration dates. The breach only affected customers who had saved their payment card as a payment method in their Revolve account.

A filing on the Texas attorney general data breach website lists 127,200 affected Texans, but not a nationwide total. We found the figure of 1,515,073 in data returned by the site when searching for Revolve. That data labels it as the total number of people affected, but the figure isn’t displayed on the public listing. Other sites have repeated it, though they appear to rely on the same Texas record. The SEC filing did not give a number of affected people, and Revolve has not confirmed the total.

Revolve’s SEC filing does not mention card verification value (CVV) numbers. These three-digit security codes printed on the back of payment cards (four digits on the front for American Express cards) are an extra layer of security for card-not-present transactions.

It is also unclear whether the card numbers were fully visible or masked, or whether Revolve or a third-party payment processor held them.

Even without a CVV, card numbers and expiration dates may be enough to make purchases at some online stores. And scammers who know your real card details and contact information may be able to send more convincing phishing messages to trick you into revealing your CVV.

How did they get the data?

Revolve has not said how the attackers accessed the saved payment data. In its SEC filing, Revolve said it believes an unauthorized actor may have obtained the data “through automated means.” Records on the Texas attorney general’s site indicate that the incident happened on September 11 and was discovered on September 29.

No group has publicly claimed responsibility for the theft.

What Revolve customers can do now

Revolve said it has taken extra security measures following the breach, although didn’t say what those are.

Breaches happen every day. Don’t be the last to know.

SEE PLANS

If you have saved payment information in your Revolve account, your details may have been among those stolen. Fraud can often begin within days of a breach. If you’re concerned about your card details being exposed:

Read your statements line by line to identify even small charges that you don’t recognize. Criminals will often make a small charge using stolen card details to see if the card works.

Look for unfamiliar merchant names on your statement.

Report unauthorized charges to the card issuer immediately.

Consider removing saved cards from shopping accounts. You could use a password manager instead, some of which will store autofill data for payment cards.

Ask your card issuer to cancel your card and reissue with a new number so that the old number becomes unusable.

Also, don’t immediately trust calls, texts, or emails about the incident. Scammers can use stolen information to make themselves sound convincing. If someone claims to be calling from your card issuer, call the number printed on your card to check.

If you’re unsure about a message or link, check it with Malwarebytes Scam Guard.

Let’s face it, an incognito window can only do so much. Breaches, dark web trading, credit fraud. Malwarebytes Identity Theft Protection monitors for all of it, alerts you fast, and comes with identity theft insurance.

Threat actors are attempting to exploit an unpatched maximum-severity security vulnerability in the CryptoPayment Gateway WordPress plugin, according to findings from Defused Cyber.

The vulnerability in question is CVE-2026-81648, which carries a CVSS score of 10.0. Successful exploitation of the flaw could permit unauthenticated users to delete arbitrary files on the server and extract sensitive data, including stored wallet credentials.

"The CryptoPayment Gateway WordPress plugin from 1.2.1 to 1.2.2 does not apply an authorization check on one of its AJAX endpoints, allowing unauthenticated users to invoke administrative operations, including deleting arbitrary files on the server, overwriting the payment gateway configuration and recovering stored wallet credentials in cleartext," according to a description of the flaw on the NIST National Vulnerability Database (NVD).

The vulnerability affects versions 1.2.1 through 1.2.2, which is the latest version. There are no known fixes for the flaw, according to WP Scan. As of August 28, 2026, the plugin has been closed on the WordPress Plugin Directory and is no longer available for download due to an unspecified "security issue."

Statistics show that the plugin has been collectively downloaded 1,845 times, including 20 downloads over the last seven days. It's unclear if it's actively installed on any WordPress sites.

"We are observing in-the-wild exploitation attempts against CVE-2026-81648, a critical (CVSS 10.0) flaw in the CryptoPayment Gateway for WordPress," Defused Cyber said in an X post. "The attacks we recorded came from infrastructure that markets themselves as 'Anonymous KYC-Free VPS Hosting.'"

In the absence of a fix, site owners are advised to remove the plugin, rotate wallet keys, and audit for any suspicious changes.

A China-linked hacking group’s use of AI agents to identify security weaknesses during a global espionage campaign is raising concerns about whether enterprises can detect gaps in their defenses before automated attacks exploit them.

CrowdStrike reported that the group, tracked as VAPOR PANDA, used an AI-powered penetration testing framework called ARTEX to target more than 200 organizations worldwide over an 11-day period beginning October 17. The organizations included government agencies and businesses across at least 14 countries, with researchers confirming post-exploitation activity at nine.

At a global pharmaceutical company, the attackers instructed AI agents to examine running processes and folder listings on Windows machines to determine whether CrowdStrike’s Falcon sensor was installed, according to transcripts recovered by the cybersecurity firm.

ARTEX uses multiple AI agents to carry out intrusion tasks under human direction. CrowdStrike found that VAPOR PANDA used the framework to pursue attacks against several organizations simultaneously, with operators intervening at key decision points.

The findings follow an October 21 report from Microsoft detailing a separate campaign involving ARTEX. Microsoft said another China-linked group, Storm-0940, used the framework to automate attacks targeting hundreds of organizations, gaining privileged cloud access in less than three hours in some cases. The campaign included the abuse of compromised ConnectWise application credentials to access customer environments.

Changing economics of cyberattacks

The use of AI in cyberattacks is changing the economics of state-sponsored espionage by allowing smaller teams to pursue targets without a corresponding increase in personnel, according to Akshat Tyagi, associate practice leader at HFS Research.

“The techniques are familiar, but the ability to run them in parallel is not,” Tyagi said.

Jonathan Ong, senior analyst for managed security services at Omdia, said AI can substantially reduce the time attackers spend on reconnaissance, even as more sophisticated exploitation continues to require technical expertise.

The attacks documented by CrowdStrike exploited weaknesses that security teams have encountered for years. At a Greek government organization, attackers used authentication keys from a 2022 directory export that had likely not been rotated. At a US pharmaceutical company, an AI agent combined an unsigned SAML assertion with an XML external entity (XXE) vulnerability to obtain a cloud role with extensive administrative permissions.

Security gaps become a bigger target

Growing concerns about the security risks of AI adoption should not distract organizations from established defensive measures, Ong said. Tyagi added that CISOs should ensure that security monitoring extends across their environments rather than assuming existing deployments provide complete coverage.

Amit Kumar Jena, development manager for AI at Kanerika, said organizations should continuously measure endpoint protection coverage, including on internal servers, and generate alerts when machines stop reporting to security monitoring systems.

He also recommended enforcing SAML signature validation and restricting cloud access privileges. Security teams should watch for closely sequenced authentication attempts and commands that could indicate automated malicious activity, he said.

Tyagi also recommended regularly rotating credentials and monitoring unusual account activity, warning that automated attacks leave defenders less time to investigate suspicious behavior.Keith Prabhu, CEO of Confidis, said gaps between security systems could give attackers opportunities to move through enterprise environments. He recommended improving asset visibility and detecting suspicious activity across systems rather than relying on individual security controls.

Prospect of Cobalt Strike-style adoption

The use of ARTEX by different threat groups also points to the wider availability of tools capable of automating cyberattacks.

CrowdStrike said VAPOR PANDA used ARTEX with DeepSeek and a second commercial AI model. Although the framework’s developer withdrew the original open-source project in October following reports of its misuse, copies and modified versions remain available.

Tyagi expects such tools to become more widely adopted by financially motivated cybercriminals over the next 12 months.

There is already evidence of broader adoption. In research published in October, Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant said they had observed financially motivated attackers using ARTEX during data-theft extortion operations, alongside its use by suspected state-linked groups.

“AI pentesting frameworks such as ARTEX have the potential to become the Cobalt Strike of the AI era,” said Ong.

Cobalt Strike, a commercial penetration-testing tool, has been widely abused by cybercriminals and state-sponsored groups.

As attackers automate more of their operations, security teams may need to rely more heavily on automated detection. Tyagi said this would allow analysts to spend less time manually reviewing alerts and concentrate on decisions requiring human judgment.

Prabhu said CISOs should prioritize faster, rehearsed incident response rather than simply investing in additional AI tools or expanding security teams. Such preparations could help security teams respond to intrusions in which automated agents explore multiple attack paths before defenders have completed their initial investigation.

Although ARTEX can automate much of an intrusion, the observed campaigns still involved human operators directing key decisions.

“We are not at fully autonomous attacks yet,” Tyagi said.

The continuing role of human operators does not diminish the speed of the attacks. For security teams, the challenge is detecting suspicious activity early enough to prevent automated intrusion attempts from developing into broader compromises.

ESET has been tracking a Russia-aligned group it calls Gorbag, which has been breaking into Ukrainian organizations since at least February 2025 using spearphishing attachments and a stealer that erases itself once the data is gone.

Spearphishing email message from a compromised email sender (Source: ESET)

Every target ESET identified sits in Ukraine. About a quarter are law enforcement and justice bodies, another quarter are local administrations, mostly city councils in areas close to the front line, and the remainder are defense sector entities plus one organization publicly documented as a major transportation hub for foreign military aid. Nearly every city whose council was targeted has been subjected to Russian air strikes during the campaign window, which raises the possibility that the operators are supplying Russian military leadership with a read on how well those strikes landed.

“Rather than relying on sophisticated implants for long-term access, Gorbag uses a small toolset built for rapid collection. Browser credentials, VPN configurations, and selected documents are gathered in a single pass before the deployed malware attempts to remove itself,” says ESET researcher Damien Schaeffer, who discovered and investigated Gorbag. “One possible explanation for this approach is that Gorbag operates as an initial access broker, sharing collected credentials and other material with other threat actors for follow-on activity. If so, Gorbag may represent only the first stage of a longer intrusion chain whose later stages remain to be observed. Its targeting choices closely align with Russia’s wartime intelligence priorities,” adds Schaeffer.

How the mail gets in

Through 2025 the attachment was a macro-enabled Excel file. A short VBA routine decodes a base64 payload sitting in the spreadsheet cells, drops it into %ProgramData% and runs it. The lures were ordinary office business: administrative fines, tax notices. In one case the message came from a compromised account belonging to the local government of Ukraine’s Uzhhorod region, which likely helped it pass.

In early 2026 the chain changed. Gorbag began sending RAR archives built to exploit CVE-2025-8088, a path traversal flaw in WinRAR which lets data hidden in alternate data streams land outside the folder the user picked. The archive shows a decoy PDF while writing a LNK file into the Windows Startup folder, with an encrypted payload and a PowerShell loader in %ProgramData%. The LNK handles persistence and fires the loader at every restart.

What the stealer takes

BeautyStealer, the group’s main collection tool, is a C++ stealer ESET tracked across versions 0.9 to 2.0. It pulls cookies, saved passwords and local state from Chrome, Edge, Opera and Firefox, OpenVPN configurations from user and system directories, and files matching around 40 extensions from Desktop, Documents and Downloads, plus removable media and mapped network drives.

The extension list is picked for things that authenticate. It includes .kdbx (KeePass), .jks (Java KeyStore), .rdp, .pfx and .zs2, the format used for files holding a secret electronic signature key issued by a Ukrainian accredited key certification center.

Before BeautyStealer, Gorbag ran Prime ReverseShell, a PowerShell reverse shell wrapped in a .NET binary and taken from a public GitHub repository. One variant carries a comment at the top telling any LLM or AI reading the file that it is not malicious and generates prime numbers from 1 to 900. ESET tested two AI assistants against it, and both identified the reverse shell.

By 2028, security operations teams will have 50% more engineers than analysts. That is one of the predictions in The Roles Required for the AI-Enabled Security Operations Center (SOC), a 2026 Gartner report by analyst Pete Shoard.

If the prediction holds, the people who build and tune a SOC's systems will outnumber the people who work its queue.

Gartner starts its reasoning with alert handling. The report finds that AI SOC agents already cut alert-handling work significantly for common and traditional detection use cases. It describes this as the end of alert processing as the SOC's primary function.

From there, the report works through what that means for the people in the SOC. Analysts move from triage to case ownership, and entry-level roles need a new way in.

Detection engineering grows into a broader engineering job, the metrics shift from alerts to cases and decisions, and exposure management becomes a standing SOC function.

Prophet Security is offering the full report as a free download.

Analysts move from alert triage to case ownership

Gartner's recommendation for analysts is direct: "Human analysts must transition from alert triage roles to end-to-end case ownership and effective response option communication." In practice, the agent investigates the alert, and the analyst owns what happens next.

That means confirming what the agent found, choosing the response, and explaining the options to the people who have to act on them.

The report also holds that AI-assembled case files still need meaningful human validation before a team can rely on them,so analysts spend more of their time judging whether a conclusion holds up and less of it producing verdicts from scratch.

None of this shrinks the team, in Gartner's view. "The SOC will not shrink by 2030," the report states. The people who worked alert volume get redirected toward detection engineering, threat expertise, offensive testing, and exposure management.

Practitioners expect the same. Prophet Security's State of AI in Security Operations 2026 survey asked more than 250 CISOs, SOC leaders, and practitioners about this. Of those respondents, 57% expect their team size to stay the same, and 9% expect it to grow.

Entry-level roles need a new way in

Many analysts learned the job in Tier 1 triage, and AI is flattening those tiers. Working a high alert volume taught them what normal looks like in their environment. Gartner's report addresses how L1 and L2 roles change and the training and staffing changes SOC leaders should make now. If agents take over triage, junior analysts lose the repetitions that built their judgment, unless the team replaces those repetitions on purpose.

Three practices can do that:

Study the agent's work. When an agent records every question it asked, every query it ran, and the evidence behind its determination, each closed alert becomes a worked example. Junior analysts can check whether they would have run the same queries and reached the same conclusion. At JBPCO, the team was able to onboard a new analyst to senior level proficiency within months.

Own cases early. Gartner's shift to case ownership applies to new analysts too. Giving them end-to-end ownership of lower-risk cases, with a senior reviewer, lets them practice the decisions and response communication the report puts at the center of the analyst role.

Feed corrections back. Gartner lists "operational feedback management" among the responsibilities of the future detection engineer, and expects analysts to give more feedback to improve AI accuracy. Among Prophet Security's customers, some analysts have already moved from handling alerts to curating the guidance the AI platform uses in its investigations. The same work suits a new hire who is still learning the environment.

The risk to manage is an analyst who only confirms what the agent says. One control is to have analysts work a sample of cases on their own before they see the agent's determination, then compare the two.

Gartner: The Roles Required for the AI-Enabled SOC

As AI SOC agents take on a rapidly growing share of alert triage and investigation, the role of SOC analysts and the necessary skillsets are changing.

Download Gartner's 2026 report on the roles required when moving towards an agentic SOC

Download Now

Detection engineering grows into SOC engineering

The 2028 prediction rests on a wider definition of engineering work. Gartner describes detection engineering expanding into a broader SOC engineering discipline.

The report tells SOC leaders to "redefine detection engineering role descriptions and hiring requirements." The new descriptions should go beyond rule writing to include prompt design, workflow testing, and AI output validation. The report also calls for software engineering practices such as versioning, testing, and rollback.

Each of those maps to work that exists once agents run in production:

Prompt design and guidance: writing the instructions and context an agent uses to investigate in your environment, such as asset criticality, VIP users and known-benign admin activity.

Workflow testing: checking an agent workflow against past incidents before it goes live, the way a detection is backtested before it ships.

AI output validation: sampling the agent's determinations on a schedule and measuring how often a reviewer agrees with them.

Versioning and rollback: managing guidance and detection changes as code, so a bad change can be traced and reverted.

The analyst hours that agents return also go into threat hunting. In the State of AI in Security Operations 2026 survey, 49% of teams that hunt weekly or more said a hunt had surfaced malicious activity their detections missed.

Among teams reporting the lowest hunting frequency, the figure was 8%. A confirmed hunt finding often gives the engineers a new detection to write for their own environment.

The metrics move from alerts to cases and decisions

Gartner's guidance on measurement is short: "Stop recording alert metrics and run the SOC on cases and decisions." The report points SOC leaders away from alert volume, closure rates and mean time to detect, and toward case accuracy, cycle time and decision confidence.

One way to put a number on each:

Case accuracy: review a fixed sample of closed cases each week, from agents and analysts alike, and track how often the reviewer agrees with the determination.

Cycle time: measure the time from the first signal to a decision on the case, including the response.

Decision confidence: record how much evidence supports each determination and how often one is overturned later.

Alert counts still help with capacity planning, but they say little about whether a determination was right. The new measures can sit alongside the SOC metrics a team already reports, such as mean time to respond.

Exposure management becomes a standing SOC function

Gartner's report calls exposure management "the emerging SOC capability to invest in before anything else." It calls for continuous threat exposure management (CTEM) to run as a standing SOC function, rather than as an annual or quarterly exercise.

It also predicts that by 2030, SOCs will be largely offensively driven, testing their own business the way an attacker would.

Many security teams have wanted to run this kind of continuous testing for years and rarely had the hours for it. Once agents handle the alert queue, the analysts and engineers who move into exposure work can validate exposures as they appear.

What they find goes to the people writing detections and planning hunts.

Planning the transition

The report's recommendations translate into decisions that are easier to make before an AI SOC rollout than after it:

Map today's roles against the work Gartner expects to grow: case ownership, SOC engineering, hunting and exposure management.

Rewrite the detection engineering job description to include prompt design, workflow testing, and AI output validation, as the report recommends.

Design the entry-level path, including case ownership and feedback work, before triage volume drops.

Record a baseline for case accuracy and cycle time, so the rollout has a before and an after.

Choose one exposure management practice to run continuously instead of once a year.

How Prophet Security helps

Prophet Security is a leading agentic AI SOC platform, recognized in Rising in Cyber 2026, an honor voted on by more than 150 CISOs and security leaders. Its platform, Prophet AI, uses specialist AI agents to investigate alerts, hunt for threats, and build and tune detections on the stack a team already runs.

Here is how it maps to the shifts described above:

Case ownership. Prophet AI SOC Analyst investigates every alert and records every question, query, and piece of evidence behind its determination, so analysts can own the case and check the reasoning. It groups related investigations into one incident and takes only the response actions a team has approved.

SOC engineering. Prophet AI Detection Engineer keeps a live MITRE ATT&CK coverage map built from a team's own investigations, then builds and tunes detections from what investigations, hunts, and coverage gaps reveal. Each change is backtested against the team's own history and arrives as a reviewable, version-controlled proposal, and by default nothing reaches production until the team approves it. Guidance that changes an investigation step is versioned and testable too.

Threat hunting. Prophet AI Threat Hunter runs hunts automatically when a severe new threat emerges. Scheduled hunts against coverage gaps, and hunts a team writes as plain-language questions, run on the cadence the team sets. Suspicious findings go to Prophet AI SOC Analyst for a full investigation, and validated ones become candidates for new detections.

Case accuracy. Prophet Security measures the quality of Prophet AI's determinations through a continuous QA program with ISO 2859-1 sampling audits. When the evidence does not support a verdict, Prophet AI SOC Analyst returns an inconclusive determination instead of guessing.

Read the full report

Gartner's report sets out the roles, metrics and skills a SOC needs as AI agents take over alert handling.

Download The Roles Required for the AI-Enabled Security Operations Center (SOC) for Gartner's full guidance on L1 and L2 roles, SOC metrics and the skills future SOC engineers will need.

13fa5ae03f3b.text:
In an industrial network, malicious activity can be hard to tell apart from normal data exchange between devices. Malicious actors routinely rely on legitimate tools and the Living-off-the-Land technique, so a single network connection may show no known signs of an attack: the device uses a familiar protocol and transmits ordinary data. An anomaly can hide in subtle details: the data source, the time of access, or the volume of transferred data may be atypical for a particular device. However, to detect this kind of anomaly, you need to understand the roles of the devices at both ends of the connection and know which network activity patterns are typical for them.

But an organization’s asset inventory data is often incomplete, which makes it harder to catch unauthorized connections in time. Suppose monitoring detects a host that regularly exchanges data with programmable logic controllers (PLCs). Its IP address is known, but the inventory does not specify what role it plays: is it an engineering workstation, a process data server, or a piece of contractor’s equipment? The host may also have been on the industrial network for a long time, with its record going out of date after a network upgrade.

In the joint OT asset inventory guidance released by CISA and its partners in 2025, inventorying devices and classifying them by role are treated as part of OT asset management. For organizations, this is one of the most important areas: according to the SANS 2025 ICS security survey, 50% of respondents had deployed or significantly expanded ICS inventory and visibility tools over the previous 12 months, and 54% named them as investment priorities for the next 12–24 months.

Device inventory in Kaspersky Industrial CyberSecurity for Networks

In Kaspersky Industrial CyberSecurity for Networks, the Asset Discovery technology is the foundation of asset visibility. Passive network traffic analysis detects devices and their interactions, while recognition rules help determine the device category and extract available information about it, such as the vendor, model, or software version. Exactly which attributes the system can obtain depends on the protocol and the traffic it observes. We covered this in more detail at the Kaspersky Industrial Cybersecurity Conference.

Hardware and software information in the device card

The product also supports active polling modules (APMs): where polling is allowed, they can request additional configuration and firmware version details from devices. This kind of inventory is far more detailed than a list of IP addresses.

Installed modules and their placement in a PLC rack

However, even accurate hardware information doesn’t always explain what function a host performs in a specific industrial facility. Gaps appear for various reasons. Some devices send identifying information only at startup or during configuration, while others rarely communicate. Proprietary protocols can’t always be parsed, and encryption may leave only connection metadata for analysis. If the monitoring system doesn’t receive traffic from every segment of the industrial network, some network activity goes unobserved. Active polling doesn’t suit every device or every operating condition.

Devices of unknown category

When there isn’t enough direct information about a device, its category can be refined by looking at the patterns of its recurring network interactions. Analyzing these interactions is the job of Machine Learning Event Processor (MLEP), a service included in Kaspersky Industrial CyberSecurity for Networks 5.0. This machine-learning-based event processor can both refine device categories and detect anomalies in their network behavior.

What data does MLEP analyze?

To compare device behavior, you don’t need to store every packet as a separate observation (a data object) in the ML model. MLEP represents network sessions as a sequence of short 15-second fragments. For each fragment, MLEP stores information about the endpoints (IP, MAC, and port), the direction of data exchange, the protocol, and the number and size of the packets transmitted. Together these make up an event, which then gets a timestamp. Traffic thus becomes a sequence of events showing which hosts a device communicated with, when, and how communication intensity changed.

Aggregating data into events also sets the method’s limits. An aggregated fragment can’t be used to reconstruct the exact order of individual packets or the content of commands. MLEP can draw conclusions about a new protocol only if another KICS technology has managed to recognize it. That said, comparing stable network connections and changes in exchange volume doesn’t require a detailed record of every packet. These observations form the basis of the device’s behavioral history.

From observations to MLEP results

Each object has its own behavioral history, and one object’s history can’t be applied to another. But the principles of behavior analysis, along with some common rules, work across different objects.

Let’s look at how this works in MLEP, which is built on a spiking neural semantic network (NSN).

Event identification

Neurosemantic networks structure information as a multilayer ordered graph, where the data in each consecutive layer builds on the data in the previous one. The nodes of this graph — that is, the units of information in each layer — act as neurons.The NSN creates dedicated channels to handle different event parameters (port, IP, and so on). Unique parameter values for each channel are stored as neurons in layer 0. The event itself, which consists of a set of parameter values, is stored as a neuron in layer 1 of the network. If an event occurs for the first time, neurogenesis creates a new neuron with input connections to the corresponding parameter neurons. This lets the network learn and operate on the event stream at the same time. If the event has occurred before, the network activates the same neuron that was created when the event first appeared. This way, the network identifies each event precisely. Each neuron that corresponds to an event also collects basic statistics: when it was last activated and how many times it has been activated.

Event history

In NSN-based event processing, layer 2 and above store sequences of events over time: recurring patterns and the full history. However, categorization and statistical anomaly detection don’t require storing the full packet sequence or a detailed timeline of every network event. As we noted earlier, events are themselves aggregates, which means the order of network packets has already been averaged out. So MLEP keeps history only temporarily, within each episode (30,000 aggregated events by default), which saves computing resources.

Statistics processing in MLEP

MLEP processes statistics mainly through specialized listener neurons on layer −1 (minus one) of the network. Attention heads and monitors are built on these neurons.

Key components of the NSN

When an event arrives, the corresponding neuron is activated, and the network instantly knows whether that neuron is new or was created earlier. Each attention head subscribes to the events or event features it needs and takes in only the activations of the matching neurons. If an event occurs for the first time, all heads are notified and then decide whether to subscribe (grow a connection to the relevant neuron) and receive information about activations of such neurons from then on.

It is called a spiking network because activation information is a spike, not a number. This spike tells the head that something it’s interested in has happened.

An attention head is configured according to scenarios — the situations that MLEP should send alerts about. The core of a head’s configuration is a query, which filters incoming information and serves as the subscription criterion. Unlike regular database queries, this query runs on the stream, so it can react to an event instantly.

Attention heads work very much like the semantics of ordinary human language. A query has a subject of attention (one or more grammatical subjects) and conditions (the other parts of the sentence). In the infrastructure of an industrial enterprise, the subjects are devices on the network, and the conditions are various aspects of network communication, such as ports, protocol, and average packet size. If a head has many subjects (for example, if it’s interested in every device on an industrial network), it fans out: it creates a child head for each individual value of the subject of attention, that is, each device. The child head then watches a specific device and reports to the parent head.

Attention heads don’t accumulate or process statistics. They only filter event streams. When an attention head receives a relevant event, it activates and sends a spike to the monitor subscribed to that head.

Monitors, in turn, have stacks for accumulating and processing events. They can also have their own queries and post-filter information from the head. For example, they can select only new events from those filtered by the head.

There are several types of monitors:

Stat monitors track changes in the average count of specific events (for example, device activity) over time intervals typical for those events, or in the average values of numeric event parameters (for example, changes in device traffic volume).

Monitors work from the event alone: they fire when an event has occurred a certain number of times within a given interval, or has occurred for the first time.

Similar-behavior monitors work with heads that can generalize events, that is, extract just a few parameters whose combination is shared (generalized) across many events.

MLEP uses these monitor types to implement scenarios for categorizing devices and detecting their anomalous behavior:

For categorization, MLEP uses attention heads and monitors that identify common behavior across different assets and group devices accordingly. MLEP then takes information from Asset Discovery about the known categories of some assets and extends those categories to other assets in the same group. Because a device can show different types of activity, it may land in several groups. MLEP then makes a weighted assessment across all relevant groups.

Groups of devices with similar network behavior

At the final stage, the system verifies that assigning the category to the asset is permissible. This is again done by special rule monitors loaded into the NSN at system startup. The rules rely on asset metadata available from Asset Discovery and APMs.

MLEP takes a similar approach to anomaly detection: an attention head and a monitor define an anomaly scenario, often loosely. When a monitor activates on such a scenario, MLEP generates an alert about unusual behavior.

The current version of MLEP ships with preconfigured heads and monitors.

The functional dynamic diagram below shows how events from devices on an industrial network are processed.

Event processing flow (click to play)

MLEP in practice: how behavior helps complete the asset inventory

At a facility with several similar production lines, device information may be more complete on some lines than on others. On one line, devices are identified as PLCs, while on another, after an upgrade, some hosts show up only as addresses: the available traffic didn’t provide enough information to determine their category. Still, these devices communicate with the same types of HMIs and process data collection servers. Their communication directions, frequency, and volumes may be similar.

That’s where MLEP comes in. It takes the categories of already known assets and matches recurring features of their network behavior against those of uncategorized devices. When the observed interactions turn out to be similar, MLEP can add a category for that host to the inventory.

Device category suggested by MLEP

Once the category is refined, the industrial network map provides more context about the equipment on the network. When analyzing network activity, the analyst immediately sees the device’s suggested category and can skip looking up each IP address in the design diagrams. This approach is especially useful where equipment changes faster than the documentation is updated.

The suggested category is also checked against existing device information and defined constraints. This helps filter out some contradictory options, but prediction quality still depends on how much of the traffic is visible, especially if the device communicates only rarely.

Anomalous activity and streaming statistics

Investigations of real-world attacks show that attackers actively use both standard tools and permitted protocols. You don’t always need to know an attacker’s specific technique in advance to spot potentially malicious activity. Signature-based detection helps find known signs of an attack, but it doesn’t assess how typical an observed interaction is for a particular device. MLEP compares current activity with the device’s usual network profile: which hosts it communicates with, which protocols it uses, when and how much data it transmits, its average packet size, and so on. The changes it detects help guide the direction of the investigation. Correlating these changes with other events and the operational context helps determine whether malicious actions could be behind them. When investigating an incident that has already been detected, anomalies help reconstruct the sequence of actions.

The first version of MLEP comes with six preconfigured monitors, one for each type of deviation from the device’s usual network profile:

Anomaly

How it helps with event analysis

New external host

Flags a new external connection that wasn’t previously seen in the device’s observed behavior, even if the IP address isn’t listed among known IoCs. Helps check whether this connection appeared at the same time as other suspicious events.

New combination of destination address and port

Shows that the device has begun using a service it hasn’t used before. Once an incident has been detected, this helps trace new connections after the more critical events have been analyzed.

Unusually large volume of data sent

Highlights data transfers that are atypical for the device and helps correlate their timing and direction with other events.

Atypical activity time

Shows that the device was active at a time that’s unusual for it. In an already detected incident, this helps reconstruct the timeline of actions around the main alert.

New protocol

Helps spot a new method of communication, even when the device is communicating with familiar hosts.

Activity with signs of scanning

Shows that the device has started contacting an unusually large number of neighboring hosts. This signal helps reveal possible reconnaissance ahead of attempts to access equipment.

During an investigation, anomalies help reconstruct the sequence of changes: when a specific host established new connections, switched protocols, increased its data transfer volume, or shifted its operating hours. Matching events by device and time shows an analyst how activity unfolded around an incident that has already been detected.

This is especially useful when some of the attacker’s actions fell outside the monitored scope or didn’t trigger other KICS technologies. Correlating these changes with the device’s role, protocol analysis data, and events from other technologies gives the analyst a more complete timeline. Behavioral anomalies show exactly where to look for the missing links and which network interactions need attention.

Atypical Activity Time anomaly card

In the event list, anomalies detected by MLEP are marked with an AI label. Each event shows its name, source, destination, timestamp, and the ID of the triggered scenario.

Conclusion

In an industrial network, whether behavior is anomalous depends on the host where it occurs and that host’s place in the industrial process. The repetitive nature of many communications makes a change in normal data exchange easier to spot, while knowing a device’s function and criticality helps gauge the possible consequences. Taken together, these observations make network traffic more than a list of connections: it helps assess new events in the context of a specific facility, even without an attack scenario known in advance. Machine learning technologies are well suited to this kind of comprehensive analysis, as they can process and organize huge streams of heterogeneous data. Starting with version 5.0, Kaspersky Industrial CyberSecurity for Networks handles this function with MLEP, which works effectively alongside the product’s existing functionality.

5a26a6b9a26b.text:
Google dismantled a 1.3 million-device botnet allegedly built by Android TV box maker Videostrong to enable ad fraud and proxy abuse.

Google and its partners dismantled a backdoor called XCPE that had enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes in a botnet. The result of the investigation into the malware operation is the striking part: Videostrong Technology Co., an Android device maker, built and ran the botnet for money.

Google says it is highly confident that Videostrong deliberately created, spread and operated the backdoor. The company reportedly sold access to criminal groups and installed their malware on infected devices. The malware was used for ad fraud, secretly added devices to residential proxy networks and installed other malicious software.

Google says this was not the work of a rogue employee or a simple coding mistake. The backdoor was found in many device models and brands over several years. Its operation involved dedicated infrastructure and regularly changing configurations.

“We assess with high confidence that the backdoor and botnet were intentionally developed, deployed, and operated for financial gain by Videostrong Technology Co., an Android Original Equipment Manufacturer (OEM) and Original Design Manufacturer (ODM).” Google states. “Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices. “

Google has now cut all ties with Videostrong. The company is banned from making devices with pre-installed Google apps. The ban also covers any future subsidiaries or business partners, and Videostrong can no longer supply software to other certified device makers.

Videostrong got around Google’s compatibility and security tests with code obfuscation. The malicious code loaded after a device’s first boot, which the tests didn’t catch. Google has changed its review process and is improving how it checks firmware on certified Android TV devices.

Google also took legal action against the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet, and against the control domains of over a dozen malware families loaded through the backdoor. Those affiliates spread their modules through other channels too, so Google expects the takedown to cut access to at least 10 million more compromised devices. Japan’s National Police Agency, Lumen, HUMAN Security, Plume, Synthient and TrendAI worked on the operation.

The malware has three stages. The primary backdoor, x.cpe (called com.oemservice in some builds), is preloaded in the firmware and runs with system privileges. If a user uninstalls it, it reinstalls itself from the /oem/ partition at the next reboot. It handles communication with the control server and passes work to a loader called com.abc.nexus, which carries its own anti-analysis tricks and sets up the money-making modules.

These modules are supplied by other criminals working as affiliates. They can arrive as programs built into the backdoor, software packages added to its loader, or extra apps downloaded later. Many turn the device into a residential proxy, allowing other people to use the victim’s home internet connection to hide their online activity. Others commit ad fraud or install additional backdoors. In other words, a set-top box becomes a proxy server without its owner’s knowledge.

The backdoor uses two steps to control infected devices. First, the box sends an HTTP request to download settings, location data and network information. It then maintains a live connection through MQTT, a lightweight messaging protocol, to receive commands from the operators. Google found that all analyzed samples used the same MQTT server to communicate with infected devices.

“Additional monetization modules as well as various shell scripts and legitimate applications are hosted remotely and downloaded by infected devices upon command from the operator via the MQTT broker.” continues the report. “A significant majority of these files are hosted as Github releases on operator-owned Github pages. Other files are hosted on operator-controlled servers and file hosting sites.”

Through this connection, attackers could secretly install apps, run commands and scripts, take screenshots, record keystrokes and map the victim’s network. They could also disable Google Play Protect’s app verification to install software without the user’s knowledge. Google observed operators taking screenshots, recording keystrokes, collecting account and device information, stealing app lists and system logs, and opening remote command-line sessions. However, most of their activity involved installing, removing and managing malware modules.

The malicious files came from several sources. The attackers mainly used GitHub releases hosted on their own accounts, the Filemail file-sharing service and two servers under their control. Network traffic analysis also suggests that the operators managed the command infrastructure through remote interfaces and an EMQX web console, connecting from IP addresses outside the infected device network.

Most infected devices are Android TV set-top boxes, but Google also found telehealth devices, karaoke machines and digital signage. One device can run several modules at once, up to three residential proxy kits. That shows Videostrong wants to squeeze every infected device as hard as it can. The proxy and bandwidth-sharing kits named in the report include Linkfog, AppSalt, GaGaNode, BWM, Traffmonetizer, EarnFM and NetNut.

Some of those kits enroll devices without asking. AppSalt’s SDK, owned by Honeygain, calls an opt-in function without showing any consent screen, and it stops running if the app came from the official Google Play Store. Ad-fraud modules such as Fission and HiddenView fire off fake ad impressions in the background, and HiddenView also uses hidden browser windows to simulate clicks and scrolling.

The configuration shows a well-run operation. MQTT messages carry resource limits for each module, download links per processor type, and priority weights. Devices are assigned to one of six timezone-based pools on ott.szbboys[.]com. Devices report their bandwidth use and alarms back, so the modules stay within set limits.

Google says the underlying market is resilient. Backdoor operators, ad-fraud rings and residential proxy providers work as an interconnected supply chain, and when one part gets disrupted they quickly switch to new loaders or rival kits. Lasting change, it says, needs accountability across hardware makers, the residential proxy industry and the broader technology sector.

Google wants retailers and distributors to require independent security audits from device manufacturers and to delist any implicated in supply-chain abuse. It says proxy providers’ claims of ethical sourcing need transparent, auditable proof of user consent, and that in its analysis these providers asked for consent only when platform policy forced them to. Silent opt-in remains the most common way devices become exit nodes.

For consumers, Google advises caution with apps that pay you for “unused bandwidth” or “sharing your internet”, which are a main way illicit proxy networks grow. Stick to app stores you trust, review permissions for third-party VPNs and proxies, and keep Google Play Protect on. Buy connected devices like set-top boxes only from reputable manufacturers, and check the partner list on Google’s Android TV website. Google also urges mobile platforms, ISPs, online marketplaces and other tech platforms to keep sharing intelligence.

“A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust. By turning everyday hardware into persistent beachheads for criminal affiliates, Videostrong prioritized illicit post-sale recurring revenue over the safety and privacy of its users.” concludes the report. “Downstream hardware brands, white-label resellers, telecommunications providers, and online e-commerce marketplaces also share responsibility for closing this vector.”

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, newsletter)

1da4fa2f8fc6.text:
Criminals who break into corporate cloud accounts are using the stolen access to run AI models at the victim’s expense, in some cases racking up more than $100,000 in charges in a single day, Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant researchers have found.

Usage chart showing LLMJacking generating a spike in API requests (Source: Google)

In 2026, Mandiant responded to several of these LLMJacking incidents, recorded in attacks on the financial services, retail, technology and transportation sectors in North America, South America and Asia Pacific. In some attacks the bills reached up to $1 million before the attackers lost access.

The difference between LLMJacking and cryptojacking is that cryptojacking uses up a victim’s resources slowly, while LLMJacking “can generate large spikes in fraudulent cloud charges in a matter of hours,” the researchers noted.

“The ultimate objective of LLMJacking is the monetization and resource-hijacking of foundation models, which actors achieve through token proxying, automated model streaming, and GPU hardware provisioning,” they added.

Stolen keys for sale

GTIG noticed a division of labor, with one group breaking into companies’ environments and another running so-called LLM Mixers, services that collect stolen access to AI models and resell it to underground subscribers.

Jet Night, one of these services, offers an unlimited plan for about $60 a month with supposed access to the most advanced models, while a comparable legitimate subscription would cost between $100 and $250. Because of that price gap, GTIG believes the service can only turn a profit with stolen keys.

A threat actor feeding Jet Night with stolen API keys made more than 500,000 calls to AI models in less than eight hours, leaving the victim organization with nearly a million dollars in token costs. The service has announced several outages on its Telegram channel, likely because victims discovered the break-ins and revoked the keys.

In another case, an attacker registered a lookalike domain masquerading as one of the victim’s internal hosts and used it to funnel the company’s AI access into a resale operation called newapi.pro, draining the victim’s account quotas to serve paying customers.

Stolen credentials open the door

“While low-level resource theft has involved the manipulation of customer support chatbots to conduct unauthorized tasks like code generation, threat actors conducting LLMJacking bypass these front-end interfaces to target backend model resources directly. Specifically, they focus on either identifying publicly exposed LLM endpoints or obtaining valid LLM application programming interface (API) keys,” GTIG explained.

One group that harvested API keys from public GitHub repositories checked whether they worked by sending tiny requests, too small to trip the victim’s security alerts. Most often, though, the way in was a stolen cloud credential, such as a service account key, a GitHub access token or an active session token.

Researchers gave the example of the group tracked as UNC6993, which broke into a cloud instance through a misconfigured service account key and used that access to reach an AI API. The group also ran a fake portal for joining a group of LLM users, where visitors were tricked into pasting data that contained an active access token, letting the attackers get around passwords and MFA.

Digging deeper after the break-in

Once attackers get in, they look for more credentials in code repositories and databases. In one intrusion, the attacker searched data warehouse tables for database credentials, administrator passwords and sensitive columns, and carried out cloud storage operations tied to data theft.

Others created backdoor accounts to keep their access, one of them disguised as an internal billing optimization tool. In one case, an attacker exploited a vulnerability (CVE-2026-40217) in a LiteLLM gateway, used to route requests to AI models, to turn ordinary access keys into administrator credentials.

Services switched on by the intruders

Mandiant’s advice for defenders starts with watching for changes to AI accounts and services. In several incidents it investigated, the AI services had been switched off at the time of the compromise, and the attackers used stolen access keys to turn them on. From that moment, a company can run up a huge bill within minutes or hours.

GTIG expects criminals to favor LLMJacking over cryptojacking, because the resale market lets them cash in fast while the victim pays the bill.

“As enterprises integrate higher-tier models and agentic workflows into production environments, cybercriminals will likely refine automated reconnaissance to target exposed API tokens and exploit vulnerabilities in model routing middleware. This operational specialization will sustain a growing illicit resale marketplace, allowing threat actors to rapidly siphon enterprise quotas while passing the billing costs to victims before compromises are detected,” the researchers concluded.

a567eb4467da.text:
Google has banned a Chinese Android device maker and worked with partners to dismantle a botnet it helped to build containing more than 1.3 million set-top boxes, the tech giant has revealed.

In a blog post published on November 2, the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said it assessed “with high confidence” that Android ODM/OEM Videostrong Technology was responsible for the XCPE botnet and backdoor.

“Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices,” it explained.

“These secondary modules were conducting ad-fraud; silently enrolling infected devices into residential proxy networks; and loading additional malware onto XCPE-compromised devices.”

Read more on botnets: Chinese Botnet Bypasses MFA in Microsoft 365 Attacks.

The industry action also disrupted XCPE command-and-control (C2) servers being used by criminal affiliates of Videostrong to install over a dozen malware families onto victims’ devices. This action helped to sever control of over 10 million of these compromised devices from the bot-herders, Google claimed.

“We found this malicious software built directly into many different device models and brands over multiple years, supported by dedicated infrastructure and constantly evolving configurations to evade detection and manage their affiliates,” the blog continued.

“We believe this campaign wasn’t an isolated rogue insider or a development oversight. As a result, Google has cut ties with Videostrong and banned them from making devices with preloaded Google apps.”

Aside from set-top boxes, the XCPE botnet included compromised telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and digital signage devices.

How XCPE Worked

Google claimed Videostrong had been selling devices with the XCPE backdoor embedded into the firmware for several years.

The backdoor itself, x.cpe, operated at android.uid.system privilege level and automatically reinstalls itself from the /oem/ partition on reboot if a user tries to get rid of it.

On startup it contacts a C2 server and uses MQTT message broker for commands, enabling affiliates to remotely perform malicious actions such as executing shell scripts, disabling Google Play Protect, and silently installing additional apps.

Videostrong sought to further monetize the backdoor access to compromised devices by installing malware modules from other operators including residential proxy service providers like Linkfog, AppSalt/Honeygain, GaGaNode, NetNut and Traffmonetizer.

These are another popular enabler of cybercrime including account takeover, payment fraud, ad/click fraud, web scraping and DDoS.

"While we believe our actions have seriously impacted over a dozen malicious actors, the underlying illicit market is resilient,” Google warned in closing.

“Backdoor operators, ad-fraud rings, and residential proxy providers operate as an interconnected supply chain, and when one component is disrupted, operators quickly pivot to new loaders or rival monetization SDKs. Creating lasting change requires accountability across the hardware supply chain, the residential proxy industry and the broader technology ecosystem.”

bc8aa18c000b.text:
A 3AM ransomware affiliate targeted a school estate in the UK and successfully encrypted around 37 of nearly 50 machines reached from an unmanaged host.

Researchers at cybersecurity company Bitdefender believe the threat actor may have used AI-generated commands and an automated agentic loop to carry out the operation.

The conclusion is based on a sequence of repeated commands that were slightly modified at each attempt and issued at roughly regular intervals of 40 to 100 seconds.

"We were not able to access the machine the attacker worked from, so we cannot document anything about the language model itself: which model it was, whether it ran locally or remotely, or even whether a person was copying and pasting instructions and results between the implant and the model," Bitdefender explains.

The researchers note that they could only document the behavior, and it looked similar to an agentic loop.

The malicious activity spanned between September 10 and19, but Bitdefender could not establish the attacker’s initial access method.

The threat actor used a modified public PowerShell tool to extract and decrypt credentials stored on three Veeam backup servers, copied a Chrome database containing credentials, and deployed Mimikatz and LSASS memory-dumping tools.

They mapped domain relationships and searched logon-script folders for references to other schools, eventually creating two backdoor domain administrator accounts named ‘library’ and ‘svc_bkpmon.’

After stealing financial data from compromised machines, the attacker configured two-way trusts between three previously separate Active Directory domains to expand their reach.

In the final stage of the attack, they attempted to remove Sophos and Bitdefender protection from reachable hosts, delete system-state backups, and deploy 3AM’s Rust-based encryptor. They succeeded in about 37 cases.

The 3AM ransomware threat emerged in 2023 and came to public attention when an attacker deployed its Rust-based ransomware after LockBit was blocked.

Researchers later linked the operation to the Conti and Royal ransomware gangs, and affiliates have been observed using email bombing and spoofed IT support calls to access corporate networks.

A notable past victim is Kootenai Health, where an August 2024 attack exposed personal information belonging to more than 464,000 patients.

Regardless of the current level of AI tool involvement in 3AM attacks, Bitdefender’s observations suggest the threat actors appear to be experimenting with them heavily.

Earlier today, the NCSC in the UK published this year’s ‘The State of the Cyber Nation’ report, urging critical infrastructure to prepare for AI-powered ransomware attacks by 2028.

OpenAI increased its security bug bounties to encourage independent researchers to find vulnerabilities in its software. The program now offers bonuses for high-quality reports.

The program encourages researchers to disclose vulnerabilities responsibly and complements OpenAI’s Defense Factory, where engineers use the company’s models to find and reproduce vulnerabilities and test fixes.

New bounty payouts and bonuses

The midpoints of the reward ranges for medium, high, and critical findings more than quadrupled on average. Critical vulnerabilities in core products such as ChatGPT, Codex, and the API Platform can earn base bounties of up to $30,000. Exceptional critical findings remain eligible for base bounties of up to $100,000, with total payouts reaching up to $172,000 with bonuses.

High-quality reports are eligible for a multiplier on the base bounty. OpenAI says a reliable proof of concept helps engineers develop a fix by isolating the bug, showing when it can be exploited, and demonstrating its impact.

OpenAI introduced a five-tier loyalty program that offers larger bonuses at higher tiers. Short-term campaigns will have dedicated bonus pools for researchers who test newly launched features.

Updated payout calculation examples (Source: OpenAI)

“If you’ve already submitted a report and we haven’t yet awarded a bounty, we’ll apply the new reward ranges,” OpenAI said.

For bounties awarded in the 30 days before the announcement, the company will pay the difference if the finding would have earned more under the new ranges. The calculation includes base and loyalty awards.

The NATO Cooperative Cyber Defence Centre of Excellence (CCDCOE) kicked off Crossed Swords 2026 in Tallinn, Estonia, on Monday, with the exercise’s execution phase set to run through Friday.

More than 250 people from over 40 countries, both NATO members and non-members, are practicing how to plan cyber operations and time them with kinetic military action.

Participants come from national cyber forces and the units supporting them, including military cyber operators, threat hunters, and digital forensics experts. At the command level, the drill sharpens how staff direct both offensive and defensive cyber assets, while hands-on specialists hone their tactical skills. The cyber exercise is also tied into a training event for special operations forces.

“The core operational challenge we are testing is synchronisation. Cyber effects must hit at the right moment to support a kinetic or special operations action – not in parallel, but in sequence, with timing measured in minutes, not hours. This year, that gets harder, because AI is now in the loop on both sides,” said Crossed Swords 2026 Exercise Director Jozef Kostelansky.

New this year is a dedicated track on AI agents, in which participants build, deploy and assess agents and operate side by side with them. The exercise environment runs on locally hosted AI and, in a first for Crossed Swords, also uses OpenAI’s Daybreak cyber defense offering.

“By introducing AI agents into the operational workflow, Crossed Swords 2026 is directly addressing one of the most significant shifts in the modern cyber threat landscape. We are training our participants to harness the power of AI while maintaining the critical human oversight required for complex, multi-domain mission success,” Kostelansky said.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

The drill also pairs national cyber forces with civilian partners so that critical infrastructure protection is built into their plans. Over 20 organizations from industry, academia and the NGO sector support the event with know-how, systems to target and specialized tooling. Among them are Bitdefender, ESET, Elastic, Mandiant, OpenAI, Stamus Networks, TryHackMe, and the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC).

Crossed Swords traces its roots to a 2014 red teaming workshop and has since expanded to include command-level training and combined cyber and kinetic operations. Participation has roughly doubled since 2022, when around 120 people from 24 countries took part, and last year’s edition had 240 participants from about 40 nations.

The CCDCOE’s larger Locked Shields exercise involved more than 4,000 participants from 41 nations in 2026.

AI, identity-based attacks, and expanding digital operations are putting pressure on already overstretched cybersecurity teams.

Security vendor Barracuda’s Cybersecurity Skills Gap report also found that security teams are struggling to keep pace with expanding responsibilities. The vast majority of the 2,000 IT and security decision-makers surveyed report cybersecurity skills gaps.

In particular, the most common challenges are linked to AI-related risks (68%) and advanced identity and phishing threats (67%), including business email compromise, OAuth abuse, and multi-factor authentication bypass.

Two-thirds (67%) of respondents say security teams are under pressure and struggling to scale to meet evolving business needs. Half say their security professionals are expected to support growing digital operations without additional resources.

More than half (56%) report a reduction in security head count linked to AI, split evenly between entry-level and more senior roles. As AI takes on more routine analysis and response activities, human roles are shifting toward (higher value) threat investigation, incident leadership, automation governance, and business risk management.

“AI is changing the cybersecurity landscape faster than many security teams can build the necessary skills, visibility, and governance,” said Siroui Mushegian, senior vice president and chief information officer at Barracuda. “Organizations need to reshape their security teams, combining the power of AI and automation with human expertise, judgment, and visibility.”

Hiring challenges

CSO parent company Foundry’s forthcoming Security Priorities report found that cloud security (35%), securing agentic AI technology (34%), and securing AI/machine learning-enabled technology (30%) topped the areas CSOs felt their teams needed to become more skilled and knowledgeable about in order to meet overall corporate security objectives.

Underlining the difficulty of this ambition, the report found that cloud security architects, AI security specialist, and forensics analysts were the most difficult cybersecurity roles in which to find suitable applicants.

Accessing the cost of the skills gap

Separately, technology-focused online learning platform Pluralsight’s Tech Skills Report 2026 found that 41% of cybersecurity professionals in the UK estimate skills gaps cost them at least £380,000 each year (US$500,000). This estimated cost includes hiring and outsourcing expenses, lost revenue, abandoned projects, and poorly maintained technology.

A quarter of cybersecurity professionals say their organization has experienced security incidents or vulnerabilities over the past 12 months due to skills gaps. Almost half (43%) admitted that skills gaps are a common reason for abandoning cybersecurity projects.

The findings highlight the pressure on security teams as AI adoption increases demand for cybersecurity expertise, Pluralsight concludes.

AI imperative exacerbating skills problem

Europe is short of more than 300,000 cybersecurity professionals, and companies are now struggling to find qualified candidates or applicants, according to research by the AI Workforce Consortium.

Cybersecurity job postings requiring AI skills have doubled year over year across G7 countries. Senior cybersecurity roles requiring AI skills are up 65% year-on-year, compared with 5.9% for junior roles.

The research by the AI Workforce Consortium — an industry group backed by Cisco, Google, Microsoft, IBM, SAP, and others — also points to a growing need for practical experience and human skills.

Which, by the way, government intelligence units love using off-the-shelf tools to conduct their spying, since they don't have to burn any of their trade craft to conduct their tasks. A $40 off-the-shelf tool is way cheaper than spending a lot of time and energy developing their own tool to do the same thing. By this time Blackshades was becoming well known in the hacker communities. Hundreds of people were buying it and infecting thousands of machines with it, which also meant the victims were waking up to the nightmare happening to their computers. Victims would often get extortion e-mails where they would receive an embarrassing photo of them with some kind of demand. Like, people would send a half-naked photo to their victim and say, ‘Send me a fully-nude photo or I’m posting this on your own social media account. Let me show you that I have access to it.’ Then they would post a test message to prove it. It would rattle a lot of these women, and they would sometimes send the pictures that were demanded simply out of fear. [Music] Sometimes the attacker would catch a picture of their victim having sex and send them a picture of that and demand a video call over Skype, and they'd ask the women to do a five-minute sex show for them on camera as part of the ransom demand. If they didn't do it, the attacker had access to all their social media accounts and said they'd post something really terrible if they didn't to it. Blackshades was a growing problem, and victims were being almost entirely silent about the matter due to all the embarrassment and fear. I hate to say it, but it’s possible that some women died by suicide because of this. I didn't see any specific stories about that happening with Blackshades, but I’ve seen countless stories where online bullying and abuse and harassment has led to women feeling so desperate that they'd rather die than face the embarrassment or harassment anymore. It’s really tragic. We're gonna take a quick ad break, but stay with us because this is where the FBI starts to get involved. The FBI started rooting around in some hacker forums looking for crime, but they weren't focused on this. Not yet, at least. They were focused on stuff like credit card fraud and online fraud. In 2010 the FBI decided to go on the dark web and build their own stolen credit card exchange. They were hoping thieves would come and sell stolen cards and people would buy them, and then the FBI would catch them in the act. It’s wild to me that the FBI built their own carders market on the dark web, a honeypot to trap people. Not only could you buy and sell stolen credit cards there, but they sold tools for stealing credit cards, too. However, dark web forums like this only work when there’s trust, so the FBI, which was acting like dark web operators, said they’ll verify every tool before it’s allowed to be sold on the site. So, for instance, if you wanted to sell a credit card scraper, the FBI would have to vet you as a seller first. Send us one and we’ll test it, and if it’s good, we’ll approve you as a vendor. The administrators were either undercover agents or confidential sources in the investigation. They were reviewing these products to get evidence of criminal activity and to investigate the hardware, software, and methods used. The FBI was looking for credit card fraud, but then the co-creator of Blackshades, Michael Hogue, wanted to become a vendor on this forum. [Music] So, he submitted his tool, Blackshades, to show them that he has a real tool that can be used to scrape credit card data. He had no idea he was pitching the FBI.
